title: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Startup Items
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Startup Items
summary: Startup items are a macOS boot mechanism in which each item is a directory under the StartupItems folder containing an executable and a configuration property list, StartupParameters.plist, that tells the system when and how to start it. They run during the final stage of boot, before any user logs in, and they run as root. The technology is deprecated and superseded by launch daemons, so the folder is not guaranteed to exist, yet it has been present by default on some macOS releases, which means a defender cannot assume the absence of the directory means the feature is unavailable. An adversary with administrative rights creates a directory, drops an executable and a property list into it, and gains code execution with elevated privilege at every startup, independent of logon and invisible in user session activity. Detection relies on file system baselining of the StartupItems path: unexpected directories, newly created executables, unusual ownership, and boot-time processes whose parent is the startup chain rather than a launch daemon or user session are the artefacts to look for.

beginner.definition: Startup items are a macOS way to start extra programs during boot. Each item is a folder holding a program and a small settings file. The system runs them near the end of boot with full administrator rights.
beginner.whyItMatters: Anything here runs as root, the most powerful account, before anyone logs in. An attacker who creates one folder keeps their code running after every restart. It is an old mechanism that many teams have stopped checking. Few people notice extra folders in a system directory they never use.
howItWorks: During the last stage of boot the system looks inside the StartupItems directory for item folders.
Each folder must hold an executable file and a settings file called StartupParameters.plist.
The settings file tells the system the item name, the program to run and the order to use.
An attacker with administrator rights creates a folder, a program and a matching settings file.
At the next boot the system registers the item and runs the program as root before logon.
Once registered, the item starts again at every restart without needing the attacker to return.
beginner.example: Think of a school caretaker who follows a printed list fixed inside the boiler room door. The list says which pumps to switch on and in what order each morning. Anyone able to add a line to that list can have the caretaker start a machine of their choosing, every single day, long before the teachers arrive.
takeaways: A startup item is a folder with a program and a settings file that runs as root at boot.
It starts before login, so it does not appear in any user session activity.
Baseline the StartupItems folder and treat new folders or programs there as suspicious.

objectives: Describe the structure of a macOS startup item and when it executes during boot.
Explain how creating a startup item gives an adversary persistence with root privilege.
Name the files and directories a defender should baseline to find startup item changes.
Contrast startup items with login hooks and launch daemons in terms of when they run.
Explain why a deprecated mechanism can still be worth monitoring on current systems.
